zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Strong finish, scattered start: Norfolk wahoo and Spencer yellowfin carry the week
subhead: The canyon run split into two speeds this week — slow mornings offshore, then a hot afternoon bite once the temp break sharpened up.
body_markdown:
Call it a B-plus week on the southern run. Monday and Tuesday were a grind — bait was thin on the meter and the marlin bite at Lindenkohl went quiet for most of the morning. But by Wednesday the fleet found the seam again, and Thursday through the weekend the canyons put up the kind of numbers that make the long ride worth it. Norfolk carried the back half of the week, Spencer held up the middle, and Poor Man's turned into the night-bite secret nobody wanted to talk about on the radio.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold as long as no tropical system knocked the warm eddy off its perch, and that's exactly how it played out. The Gulf Stream filament that's been parked off the shelf edge stayed put, the water stayed clean and blue, and the exotic mix — yellowfin, some bigeye, mahi, wahoo, and a scattering of white marlin — kept working the edges where that warm water folds against the canyon walls.

Spencer, out around the 38°34'N, 73°37'W range, has been the most consistent stop for boats running out of Cape May. The chunk bite there set up nicely once the current started ripping across the 100-fathom curve — butterfish chunks on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders, no weight, drifted back in the slick, and yellowfin in the 30-to-50-pound class came up steady through the afternoon. Mornings were slower, more like two or three fish before the sun got high, but the afternoon bite tightened up as the thermocline pushed the tuna shallower. A few boats working the troll early with green machines and small Islanders picked up mahi in the 8-to-15-pound range on the color changes north of the canyon head — nothing epic, but a solid bonus while waiting on the chunk to turn on.

Lindenkohl, up around 38°50'N, 73°22'W, was the disappointment early in the week — the white marlin that had been showing on the temp break went quiet Monday and Tuesday, likely pushed by a shift in the current line. By Thursday they were back, feeding on the surface in the mid-afternoon, and boats trolling a spread of horse ballyhoo behind Sea Witch skirts, staggered short and long, raised fish steadily in that 78-to-79-degree water where the break sharpens. Drop-back conversions were the difference-maker — hook baits rigged light so the circle hook could do its job on the pitch. Yellowfin showed there too, mixed in on the edge, but Lindenkohl this week was really a marlin story more than a tuna one.

Poor Man's, tucked in around 38°26'N, 73°48'W, turned into the bigeye play for boats willing to stay out after dark. The daytime bite there was spotty — a few yellowfin on the troll, nothing to write home about — but the overnight chunk with squid strips and glow sticks on the swim baits produced bigeye in the 80-to-150-pound class for boats that committed to staying on the drift through the middle of the night. That's a small window and it takes patience, but for boats set up for it, Poor Man's has been the highest-value stop per hour on the water this week.

Norfolk, the furthest run out of Cape May and Ocean City at roughly 37°23'N, 74°38'W, closed the week out strong. The wahoo bite there turned on hard Thursday and held through the weekend — high-speed spreads pulling Ilander/ballyhoo combos and cedar plugs at 14 to 18 knots across the canyon edge picked off wahoo in the 30-to-50-pound range, with a few pushing bigger. That canyon has been running warmer than the others, and the water color out there has stayed a clean cobalt blue that the wahoo clearly like. Bluefin showed up scattered in the mix, mostly smaller school fish in the 40-to-60-pound range, taking green machines off the long rigger.

The moon's building toward full over the next several days, and that's going to matter. Expect the tide push to tighten up bait concentrations along the canyon edges, which should sharpen the afternoon bite pattern that's already working at Spencer and Norfolk. If the current stays organized and the water color holds, the next 48 hours look like more of the same — strong afternoons, spotty mornings, and the chunk bite as the more reliable play over the troll until the fish commit harder to the surface.

The wildcard heading into the Labor Day stretch is the tropics. Nothing organized is close enough to worry about yet, but any system spinning up in the western Atlantic is the one thing that could scramble this eddy structure fast. Boat traffic is going to spike over the holiday weekend regardless, so expect more competition on the better drifts at Spencer and Lindenkohl. If there's only one shot to take this week, Norfolk's wahoo bite and Spencer's afternoon chunk are the two plays worth the fuel — just keep an eye on the tropical outlook before committing to the long run south.
